Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images Donald Trump Trump again rebukes Jeanine Pirro over reflecting pool ‘vandalism’ case President attacks ‘terrible mistake’ of US attorney, who said in court filing damage stemmed from botched renovation Maya Yang Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.51 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump has doubled down on his criticism of Jeanine Pirro after the US attorney for the District of Columbia publicly challenged his claims that vandals had damaged the recently renovated Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. “She said there was no vandalism. There was tremendous vandalism,” Trump told NBC News on Thursday. “So, she made a terrible mistake. I don’t understand why she did such a stupid thing.” On Friday, Pirro – a former Fox News host and longtime Trump ally who he handpicked to serve as the top prosecutor for the nation’s capital – moved to dismiss vandalism charges against a former Olympian and three others in connection with incidents at the reflecting pool. In a 20-page court filing, Pirro’s office wrote that the damage to the concrete-bottomed tourist attraction was the result of a “botched” renovation – “not vandalism”. View image in fullscreen The Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool in Washington on Wednesday. Photograph: Eric Lee/Reuters Asked on Thursday whether he would consider replacing Pirro, Trump told NBC: “I think she made a terrible decision. That doesn’t mean change.” The comments came after a reportedly heated Oval Office meeting on Monday with Trump, Pirro, and interior secretary Doug Burgum. According to the New York Times, Pirro accused Burgum of misleading the president about the rushed renovation by a vendor awarded a no-bid contract from the interior department. Later that evening, Trump told reporters he had not “made a determination” yet as to whether Pirro would be ousted. The White House did not immediately reply to a request for comment. Earlier this week, Trump accused Pirro of having “folded like an umbrella” after the justice department dismissed the case against David Hearn, a former Olympic canoeist who faced a felony property destruction charge that carried a potential sentence of up to 10 years in prison and a $1,000 fine for the act of having touched a chunk of the pool’s newly peeled coating. Hearn, 67, pleaded not guilty. In a statement after the charges were dropped, Hearn’s lawyers said the case should never have been brought, and argued that its dismissal “does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong”. “The administration owes Mr Hearn an apology,” they said. Hearn is one of seven people who was charged in connection with what Trump claimed were attempts to vandalize the $15m renovation of the reflecting pool that has been plagued by problems the justice department said was “the result of flawed installation by the contractor”. “Frankly, I think she choked,” Trump said from the Oval Office on Monday. An attorney for Hearn has since said that “ all options are on table ” for legal action. Those include “civil suits, bar referrals for the prosecutors involved, request for sanctions, and reimbursement of attorneys’ fees and expenses,” Hearn’s attorney Steven Levin said on Tuesday. Photograph: Frank Franklin II/AP United Nations Alarm at UN over sanctions threatened by US on international criminal court Group calls for proper enforcement of ICC rulings as Trump administration widens attacks on court Patrick Wintour in New York Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.33 EDT Last modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US threat to impose sanctions on the international criminal court (ICC) as an institution, not just its leading judges, could fundamentally disrupt its operation and needed to be resisted, a coalition of countries to defend international law heard at the United Nations on Friday. Ronald Lamola, South Africa ’s foreign minister, issued the warning at an event during the UN general assembly called to protect the system of international law from a growing array of threats, including open flouting of its tenets and rulings by Israel . The meeting was organised by the Hague Group, of which Lamola is co-chair, and which was set up in 2025 to protect international law and to call for the proper enforcement of the rulings of its two primary bodies: the ICC and the international court of justice (ICJ). Leaders join push to create UN body to tackle ‘awful reality’ of inequality Read more Lamola told the gathering that the US had already sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, but was now planning sanctions against the ICC itself. “If imposed, such measures could fundamentally disrupt its operations,” he said. “An independent court remains independent only if judges and officials cannot be punished for carrying out their mandates.” The head of the ICC, Judge Tomoko Akane of Japan, was sanctioned by the US in August, along with senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, for engaging in the ICC’s efforts to “prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction”. The attack on Akane was condemned this week by the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi. The US has admitted it seeks to dismantle the Hague-based ICC. In his address to the UN general assembly this week, Donald Trump once again criticised the “out of control” court, which he smeared as an “evil group of people” and urged other nations to reject. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio , has accused the court of being “a corrupt and fatally politicised supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate. We will not tolerate its assault on state sovereignty.” The next step by the US is likely to be to impose secondary sanctions on anyone who cooperates with the court, as opposed to sanctioning its senior judiciary. A designation of the whole institution would reach every European bank, insurer and technology supplier serving the court, which sits in the Netherlands . The Dutch government, as the host of the ICC, is taking the lead in trying to warn the US away from the effective immobilisation of the court. The Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten, told the UN general assembly: “International law either works for everyone or for no one. This court was established to protect us against impunity and it was built on the foundations of the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials. And now, with the ICC under attack, the writing is truly on the wall. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “After all, how can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes? And I believe there can be only one response: to say, hands off the ICC and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order.” William Schabas, a specialist in international law, noted to the meeting the irony that the resort to international law and courts was increasing dramatically even as the institutions were under attack. He said nations needed to strengthen the ICC, including by ensuring positions are not traded and only the highest calibre judges are elected. Diana Buttu, the prominent Palestinian lawyer, was among many to complain of western powers’ partial resort to international law. “The greatest threat to international law is not the state that openly defies it,” she said. “The greatest threat is our selectivity – the quiet decision that is made in capitals and rooms that the rules don’t bind everybody, they only bind some. It is the belief that we can excuse some because they are our allies, our partners and our friends.” Explore more on these topics United Nations International criminal court International court of justice Trump administration Donald Trump Marco Rubio Israel news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.jpost.com/history/article-91.text: On an overcast London morning in February 1964, Satmar hassid David Eliahu Brand passed by the Westminster Reform synagogue. Looking for work as a sofer (scribe), Brand took a chance and knocked on the front door. Ruth Shaffer, a native of Warsaw, Poland, and the coordinator for the Westminster synagogue Torah restoration project, answered the door.Speaking in his native Yiddish, Mr. Brand asked her: “Es gibt Torahs?” Do you have any Torah scrolls that have to be repaired? Ruth replied in the affirmative, but added that the synagogue possessed not just one scroll, but 1,564 Torah scrolls that had been rescued from Czechoslovakia after the war.After that astounding revelation, Ruth introduced Brand to the synagogue's spiritual leader, Rabbi Dr. Harold Reinhart. Thus began the most unlikely arrangement between a Satmar hassid and a Reform synagogue that would last for 27 years!The story begins: Demise of Jewish communities of Czechoslovakia, Moravia and Bohemia: March 15, 1939On March 15, 1939, Nazi German troops violated the Munich Agreement and marched into the capital city of Prague. This began the official annexation of Czechoslovakia. Wherever German troops entered, the Jewish communities were in danger as well.Until 1939, the Jewish communities of Czechoslovakia, Moravia and Bohemia numbered over 120,000 Jews and boasted over 350 synagogues, including the famous Maharal synagogue in Prague.Prague was also the home of the Old-New Synagogue, which was built in the year 1270, and the Pinkas synagogue, built in 1479.Almost overnight, Jews were stripped of their civic rights, banned from most jobs (including the medical field), and children were expelled from all public schools.Then, in July 1939, the Nazis established the Central Office of Jewish Emigration in Prague (directed by Adolf Eichmann), thus forcing many to abandon their communities, leaving behind their beautiful synagogues (containing hundreds of Torah scrolls) and houses of study.The first miracle: Gathering all Torah scrolls and artifacts to the Prague Jewish MuseumThe Prague Jewish Museum was built in 1906 and in 1939 was under the directorship of Dr. Karel Stein and curator Alfred Engel. Fearing that the holy and beautiful Torah scrolls in the hundreds of Czech Jewish communities would be totally lost, Stein and Engel asked permission from Nazi authorities to centralize all Jewish ritual objects in Prague in order to protect them from widespread plundering.Over 1,800 Torah scrolls and 212,000 artifacts were transferred to the museum.Whether the Nazi intent was merely to amass valuable silver and gold for its treasury or to build a museum to recall an extinct race (once all Jews would be murdered) is a matter of question, but nonetheless all of the Czech Torah scrolls and artifacts were brought to Prague.There, many Jews were employed to sort, catalogue, and store all the items that arrived from over 100 synagogues in Czechoslovakia, Moravia and Bohemia. Tragically, almost all of the employees were later deported to Terezin and other death camps and perished during the Shoah.The second miracle: Procurement of the Torah scrollsFollowing the end of World War II, the Torah scrolls lay abandoned and unattended for almost 20 years in a damp, moldy warehouse in Prague.That all changed with a tap on the shoulder in 1963. A British art dealer, Eric Estorick, was approached by a representative of the Czech State Agency to purchase some ritual objects that had been kept in storage. The Czech government, then under Communist rule, was badly in need of money and felt that this was a golden opportunity.Estorick contacted Ralph Yablon, a British philanthropist and member of the Westminster synagogue in London. Yablon consented to provide the £30,000 necessary for the purchase and shipping of all the Torah scrolls and other religious objects that had been stored away for so long.Yablon, aware that many of the scrolls were badly in need of repair, contacted his rabbi, Harold F. Reinhart, in order to determine which scrolls were totally unusable and which could be designated for restoration.Finally, on February 7, 1964, two enormous trucks carrying the 1,800 stained and tightly packed scrolls arrived in London. The original idea was that these Torah scrolls would be repaired and then returned to the communities from which they came.But soon after their arrival, it was determined that almost all of the former Czech shuls were either destroyed or the communities no longer existed.The third miracle: Restoration of the 1,800 scrollsBy the early part of 1964, all of the Torah scrolls and hundreds of other religious objects (including 400 wimples or binders) arrived in the Westminster synagogue. That is when the divine hand of God directed David Brand to knock on the door of the synagogue.As in the book of Shir Hashirim, which says: “the voice of my beloved knocks,” it was a most unlikely but divinely ordained moment. That is when the major work began in order to determine how many of the scrolls could actually be repaired.Of the total of 1,800 scrolls, Brand, along with other professional scribes, slowly and meticulously determined that hundreds could simply not be repaired-the decades of storage in horrible conditions had made many unusable.It should be noted that even if one letter of a Torah scroll is written incorrectly or if the ink dries up, the scroll cannot be used at all until repaired. Imagine what happened to the Czech scrolls when they were not used or opened for so long.The fourth miracle: Founding of the Memorial Scrolls TrustOf the entire collection of the 1,800 Torah scrolls, 1,564 were deemed to be usable, but then the decision had to be made as to how they would be used and to whom they would be given. In 1964, after several months of meticulous work by the scribal team, Ruth (1910-2006) took over the directorship of the Memorial Scrolls Trust (MST).Ruth would spend almost 40 years managing, documenting, and distributing the scrolls to communities worldwide. Amazingly, the initial filing and tracking were done on index cards only, and only many years later was the entire system transferred to a digital database.One of her early decisions was that each scroll would be given to a community or synagogue on permanent loan in order to memorialize the communities from which they came originally. In addition, since the Torah is described as a “tree of life,” the scrolls would be read and would become a living memory for all the communities that were destroyed during the Holocaust.About six months ago, I contacted the MST to find out more information about the scrolls and where they are today. I was fortunate that Jeffrey Ohrenstein, MST trustee and chairman, wrote back, and so began a series of discussions and amazing stories.Jeff said the oldest known scroll in the collection is one from the 13th century, and that today about 150 scrolls still remain in the museum in London. Over 1,400 Torah scrolls have been loaned out to communities around the globe, including 1,000 to the US, as well as Israel, Italy, Argentina, Chile, and the UAE (Dubai).Over the last 62 years, these communities have become part of the ongoing memorial to the former Jewish centers, but they have also transformed the Torah scrolls into living and eternal messengers of all who perished at the hands of the Nazis.The scrolls are not stored in the holy ark, but are read and celebrated everywhere where they have been adopted.Like the famous and tragic death of Haninah ben Tradyon (tractate Avodah Zarah 18A), when he is asked by his students what he saw as he was being tortured by the Romans, he replied: “The parchment is burnt, but the letters are flying heavenward.” Those letters, he was saying, are eternal; they can never be destroyed by our enemies.In the case of the Czech collection, both the scrolls and its holy letters have survived, been lovingly cared for, and preserved for eternity.
